record.paper_title: Lower Bounds for Unrestricted Boolean Circuits: Open Problems
record.original_question: Which Boolean functions avoid the mass production effect, meaning that for the function r × f obtained by applying f to r independent input blocks, the circuit size of r × f is not much smaller than r times the circuit size of f?

evidence.quote: For a positive integer r and a function f ∈ Bn, by r ×f we denote a function from Brn,r that applies f to r independent blocks of size n. We say that a mass production effect occurs for f when gates(r × f) is (much) smaller than r · gates(f).
What are the functions avoiding mass production effect?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a positive integer n, let B_n denote the set of Boolean functions f : {0,1}^n → {0,1}, and let gates(f) denote the minimum number of gates in an unrestricted Boolean circuit (over the full binary basis) computing f. For positive integers r and n and a function f ∈ B_n, define r × f : {0,1}^{rn} → {0,1}^r to be the function that applies f independently to r disjoint input blocks of length n, producing r output bits. One says that the "mass production effect" occurs for f when gates(r × f) is much smaller than r · gates(f); equivalently, computing r independent copies of f is significantly cheaper than computing r separate copies. 

Characterize, or exhibit explicit examples of, Boolean functions f that avoid the mass production effect: that is, families of functions f for which gates(r × f) = (1 - o(1)) · r · gates(f) (or, more strongly, gates(r × f) ≥ r · gates(f) - o(r · gates(f))) as r grows. In particular, identify structural properties of f that force the circuit complexity of r × f to grow essentially linearly in r times the circuit complexity of f, with no asymptotic savings from computing multiple independent copies in parallel.
artifact.status_search_result: The mass production phenomenon, going back to Uhlig (1974) and Paterson–Valiant, shows that for many Boolean functions r × f can be computed with only slightly more gates than f itself. Characterizing functions that avoid this effect is a recognized open problem in unrestricted circuit complexity; standard references (Jukna's "Boolean Function Complexity" and surveys on circuit lower bounds) discuss mass production but do not provide a characterization of functions for which it fails. No resolution was found in the literature.

status_evidence.title: Boolean Function Complexity: Advances and Frontiers (Jukna)
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses Uhlig-type mass production results and the gap between gates(r × f) and r · gates(f).
status_evidence.claim: Mass production is a well-known phenomenon, but no characterization of functions avoiding it is known.

status_evidence.title: Quantum Mass Production Theorems
status_evidence.snippet: Techniques are based on Uhlig's 1974 mass production theorem for Boolean functions.
status_evidence.claim: Mass production results are foundational; identifying functions that avoid them remains unresolved.
